blocks.text: Let x < y be a qualifying non-adjacent sorted pair. Every value between them partitions y - x into adjacent nonnegative gaps, so at least one of those gaps cannot exceed the whole distance and therefore is also at most D. Testing all adjacent gaps is complete. Comparing only selected neighbours or preserving arbitrary input adjacency can miss the local gap that witnesses existence.

blocks.text: Sorting by (score, recordId) makes every equal-score class contiguous and orders its IDs ascending. Therefore the first two records in a run form that run's lexicographically smallest valid pair; later members cannot improve its first ID, or its second ID when the first is fixed. Different score runs can have unrelated ID ranges, so the earliest run in score order is not necessarily the global lexicographic winner. The scan must keep the smallest candidate pair seen across all runs.

Raw sorted positions and aggregate frequencies cannot identify which source occurrences were chosen.

blocks.text: A fixed frequency array visits each input once and then inspects a bounded domain. It computes exactly the required predicate while using constant space with respect to n. Sort-then-scan is valid, but not automatically preferable. The choice changes if the domain is huge, memory is constrained, or ascending output is required; those conditions are absent here.

blocks.text: The scan contributes n - 1 constant-time comparisons, so its cost is Θ(n). Adding it to the stated Θ(n log n) sort yields Θ(n log n + n) = Θ(n log n), matching the offered O(n log n) bound. Space depends on the concrete sort implementation and is intentionally not checked.

O(n) omits the comparison-sort preprocessing. O(n²) is a valid loose upper bound for ordinary n but is not the tightest offered bound and implies quadratic work that this sort-plus-scan algorithm does not perform.

blocks.text: A globally minimum scalar gap must appear between neighbours, and duplicate values form an adjacent equality boundary. In two dimensions, points close in Euclidean distance can be separated by many points with intermediate x-values, so an adjacent-x-only scan is incomplete. Numeric ordering also gives no monotone rule for XOR equality. The transfer test is the proof of candidate locality, not the visual presence of sorted data.
